original_value: BackgroundDe novo genome assembly relies on two kinds of graphs: de Bruijn graphs and overlap graphs. Overlap graphs are the basis for the Celera assembler, while de Bruijn graphs have become the dominant technical device in the last decade. Those two kinds of graphs are collectively called assembly graphs.ResultsIn this review, we discuss the most recent advances in the problem of constructing, representing and navigating assembly graphs, focusing on very large datasets. We will also explore some computational techniques, such as the Bloom filter, to compactly store graphs while keeping all functionalities intact.ConclusionsWe complete our analysis with a discussion on the algorithmic issues of assembling from long reads ( e.g., PacBio and Oxford Nanopore). Finally, we present some of the most relevant open problems in this field.

result.paraphrase: Background: de novo genome assembly is based on two graph types, de Bruijn graphs and overlap graphs. Overlap graphs underpin the Celera assembler, whereas de Bruijn graphs have become the main technical approach over the past decade. Together, these two graph types are known as assembly graphs. Results: in this review, we examine the latest progress in building, representing, and traversing assembly graphs, with an emphasis on very large datasets. We also discuss computational methods such as the Bloom filter for compactly storing graphs while preserving all functionality. Conclusions: we end with a discussion of the algorithmic challenges of assembling long reads, for example from PacBio and Oxford Nanopore, and then present some of the most important open problems in this area.
